title: Polynesians crossed the Pacific with no compass, map or sextant
body: Over many centuries, Polynesian voyagers in double-hulled canoes reached nearly every habitable island in a triangle spanning Hawaiʻi, New Zealand and Rapa Nui, across thousands of kilometers of open ocean. They navigated by reading the sky and the sea, with knowledge passed down orally. New Zealand, probably settled in the 13th or 14th century, was among the last major lands on Earth reached by humans.

slides.heading: A compass made of stars
slides.text: Navigators memorized where dozens of stars rise and set on the horizon. Steering toward a rising star, then the next one to rise there, holds a course all night.

slides.heading: Reading the swells
slides.text: Under clouds, they felt ocean swells through the hull. Islands bend and reflect swells, so a changed pattern can betray land beyond the horizon.

slides.heading: Follow the birds
slides.text: Terns and noddies fly out to fish at dawn and return to land at dusk. Sailing the way they head in the evening points toward an island.

slides.question: In what year did the canoe Hōkūleʻa sail from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with no instruments at all?
slides.explanation: 1976. Guided by the Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug, the crew found Tahiti with no compass, chart or sextant, showing that such voyages could be deliberate rather than luck.

slides.heading: The 1976 test

slides.question: How could ocean swells reveal an island beyond the horizon?
options: Islands bend and reflect the swells
Swells always run away from land
slides.explanation: Navigators felt the swells through the hull. Islands bend and reflect them, so a changed pattern can betray land that is still out of sight.
